utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Case IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We are on Tuesday, 27 February 2007. Welcome, Witness. We are going to continue our work and without wasting any more time, I'll give the floor to Mr. Registrar if there are any IC numbers. There are none. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, and to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Praljak. Sir, if I could just go back and pick up on a couple of points from yesterday, please, before moving forward. Returning to the 9th of May for one question or two, of 1993, the people who were -- that came to the Heliodrom prison that day and the days thereafter, can you tell the Judges whether any of the people who came -- who came or were brought to the prison during that time, were any of them Serbs or Croats, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were only Muslims in that group -- in those groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We also discussed yesterday about the classification or separation of the prisoners that were brought to the Heliodrom from the 30th of June forward.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I recall correctly, or can you tell us -- let me just ask it this way: Can you tell us when you recall -- first, you or Mr. Bozic first having any list that separated the various persons who were being held at the Heliodrom prison after the 30th of June 1993, when you first had any list that separated these people into different categories as either military detainees in a way we were using the term yesterday or as prisoners of war or as civilians? When did you first have any such list that you felt was reliable or something that you could actually use to administer the prison?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in the middle of September when there were massive releases and when everybody was released except those against whom criminal reports had been filed, that was the first time when we had those people as prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, when we talked about the -- these large releases, the massive release is the term you just used, are you talking about that in association with the time when various of the HVO prison camps were closed at the end of 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. You keep mentioning the word -- the month September. Sir, can I ask you just again thinking -- think on that further. Did that happen in September or in December?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Larger releases began towards the end. I can't tell you the exact month, but I know it was towards the end of the year. I think it was in October, November. That's when the largest numbers were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, perhaps we'll come back to that with some specific documents as we continue on with your testimony. Now, I have a similar question for you. Apart from the list, the preparation of the list that were done as to categories or classification of prisoners, my next question is related not to the listing but to the actual treatment of the prisoners in terms of whether they were maintained separately, held separately at various parts of the complex after the 30th of June, 1993, and just as a refresher from yesterday, we're talking about the prison building, the school, and the sports hall. So keeping those three buildings in mind, can you tell us at what point, if at any time, during 1993 the different categories of prisoners, military detainees, prisoners of war, civilians, were held and administered separately?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the time. First of all, I'd like to focus on the prison building. There was a separate area that was physically separated, housing military detainees and prisoners. In that other part of the building there were prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how about --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And at the top of the building there were several women who were again physically separated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And how about at the school?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The school was a building that was not created as a prison, so that the premises were used to accommodate them. And there was also an infirmary there where two Muslim doctors worked. Plus, the building was fitted with bathrooms and toilets and running water. The third building or, rather, gyms and halls were right next to the school building. Again, those premises were not created as a prison. They were just used to put up the people that had been brought in. In the gym, again, there was running water, a toilet, a bathroom throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me -- let me stop you there, sir. As to each of the two other buildings, the -- let's start first again with the school. My specific question was: Was only one category of prisoners, the types of persons we were discussing earlier this morning, was only one type of prisoner held at the school or were there various types of prisoners held at the school?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the school only one category of people were kept, those who were brought in after the 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And among those people -- was there a classification of the people brought in after the 30th of June as detainees, prisoners of war, or civilians?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We at the prison were not aware of who was a prisoner of war and who was a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can I ask the similar question, then, about the sports hall. Were those people all of one -- were those prisoners, the people being held -- let me use a general term. The people that were being held there, were they of one category or was there any separation or classification of the people held in the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was the same as in the school building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And these are the people -- is it correct from what you told us yesterday, the people in particular in the school building and in the sports hall were those that were separately received and processed by Mr. Vidovic and his group around the 30th of June; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And just before we move on, since you touched on it, you said there were two Muslim physicians or medical people at the school. Is it correct, sir, that these Muslims were themselves detainees or prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, if we can go forward, and if I could direct your attention to Exhibit P 03411. We were talking -- we ended the day yesterday talking about the interrogation of prisoners. Do you have that, please?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you give me the number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, of course. 3411. If you have that, sir, can you just look at that for a moment and tell the Judges what this document is, please. Do you recall, sir, that around the 12th of July, 1993, some new procedures were put in place concerning people held at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And this document, Exhibit P 03411, does that set out as you best recall it what those procedures were at that time, or the rules, if you will?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Zvonko Vidovic was appointed from the crime prevention service, and after he wrote his instructions, I think this was complied with except in exceptional situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Around this time, did you also have any knowledge of or involvement with a man named Zara Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know Zara Pavlovic, but I heard from Mr. Stanko Bozic about Zarko Pavlovic, concerning the releases he made and his powers, that he was in charge of the area of Capljina, and that he was authorised for those prisoners as far as their releases were concerned and as far as future work was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And so the record is clear, when I hear you say he was responsible for those prisoners, are you saying he was responsible for the prisoners coming from the Capljina area?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not in charge inside the prison, but he was in charge of further procedure and of all decisions concerning them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you know from what organisation or authority Mr. Pavlovic came from?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was an official of the SIS or perhaps the crime prevention service, one of these two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, moving forward, did you also -- can you tell the Judges whether you also heard at this time, as these procedures were being put in place, what the continuing role of Mr. Pusic, Berislav Pusic, would be in connection with the release of prisoners, things we were talking about yesterday afternoon?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Berislav Pusic was an official of the military police administration until I think July when he was appointed head of the office for exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what role after that point, after his -- after he became the head of the office for exchange, what was his role in the release of prisoners from the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the chief or, rather, the head of the office for exchanges, he had powers over the detained prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to turn to Exhibit 3351. And if you can find the section in that document, that is the section numbered 2.4. Do you have that? In the B/C/S version, sir, there's a page that -- the top of the page starts with heading 2.4. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If you can look at this for a moment, please. Sir, this document appears to be a report of the HVO military police administration for the first six months of 1993, January to June 1993. Can I ask you, if you're looking at 2.4, just directing your attention to couple of -- a couple of the sentences there. The first sentence: "Over 6.000 prisoners of war have been held in prisons in Herceg-Bosna over the past period. Currently there are over 4.000 prisoners in prison. Of this number, several hundred are members of the Serbian army, and the overwhelming number are members of the army of BH. "Prisoners are taken out for work in large numbers, this making it possible for them to escape. "There have been a number of such cases but there exists no possibilities for increasing the number of military police." Based on your experience and your involvement at the Heliodrom prison at the time this report was written, is that information consistent with what you knew or understood to be the case at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't have much to say about this except perhaps one thing. There was a large number of people, how large I don't know, but it's probable that somebody qualified, competent, made this report. As for the number of military policemen who worked as guards, it was a very small number, and they never sent us the reinforcements that we had requested. As I said, officers of the SIS and the crime prevention service did their jobs and worked every day with the detainees and prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the last sentence of that section it says: "Instances" - excuse me - "Instances have been reported of forcible entry into prisons and forcibly conducted investigations on the part of some commanders. Such practices should be definitely forbidden and prevented."

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall a single such case where I was present during such a forced entry, but if it's written in the report, then probably there were reports to that effect and maybe it did happen, but I didn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that there were not sufficient number of military policemen. The reinforcements that we had requested were not provided. Is that an issue that you, Mr. Praljak, raised on a number of occasions, that there were insufficient military policemen at the Heliodrom prison?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall a particular --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I must have a question of understanding. I don't really understand this: Forcible entry. If it means that people were sent to prison against their will, that is a rather normal practice. What is forcible to be understood as meaning in this context here? I don't know whether the witness or the Prosecution will answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will defer in the first instance, of course, Your Honour, to the witness if he can assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you understand the Judge's question, Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I can only clarify what's written here. As far as I understand it, forced entry or forcible entry was made by other units, and people were taken out by force to be investigated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the language, just to pick up and to follow up on Judge Trechsel's question, the language of the report, at least as its translated in English, is the reports of forcible entry into prisons. I don't think bringing people forcibly to the prisons, but forcible entry into the prisons and forcible --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Here in the translation it says that certain commanders forcibly entered and conducted investigations --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- of prisoners of war or other people who were inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Before we continue on to another aspect related to this, Mr. President, we're move off or forward from some of the evidence that we expect to obtain from this witness concerning the matter of releases and the documentation of that. A larger amount of those materials is part of the various bundles that have been prepared in connection with the witness, this witness. Bundles 1, 2, 5, 6 and 12 are all bundles of collections of documents all related to the release of prisoners during this time, and if time allows at the end of his testimony, we will have -- we'll ask the witness to further confirm these bundles of exhibits, but I'm just informing the Chamber now that that is the way we're prepared to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Scott. We are dealing with documents 33, 51, and I have to ask certain questions. At 2.4, it is said that there were hundreds of soldiers who were members of the Serb army. It's the first time I see this reference. To the best of your knowledge, when you were deputy warden of the prison, were there Serb soldiers detained and, if so, were they mixed in with the Muslims? Where were those Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the report relates to 1993 and the month that is indicated, we did not know among those 6.000 people mentioned here who was of Serb ethnicity, who was a Muslim, or any other ethnicity. Only Mr. Vidovic and his group knew that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You surprise me. In a -- so far as you explained that the prisoners of war were separated from the soldiers and others. Now, I assume, but this is a hypothesis, that those Serb prisoners were prisoners of war. Were they not? And if they were prisoners of war, how come you weren't kept abreast of that and didn't know about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How would I know about it from the 30th of June when they were brought in if we had no insight into the names, the first or last names of any of the people who were brought in? The number is known, the number before the 30th of June, and then there are reports about how many military detainees there were and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. There's no point in going further. Now, my last question -- yes, Mr. Coric. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to be of assistant here. I think that something has been omitted. The Prosecutor should have said that this is an excerpt from a six-month report from the 1st of January, 1993, until the 1st of July, 1993. So these are facts and figures for six months, the first six months of 1993. And in that first stage in 1993, most of the prisoners in the prison were Serb, Serb prisoners, and then the situation changed. I want to help the witness out here for him to be able to give the proper answer as it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That will allow us to have a better understanding of the sentence. And now my last question for this witness just now. In the Naletilic trial that was tried here, and we admitted certain facts, it emerged that Mr. Mladen Naletilic came to the prison in order to assist in the interrogations. Now, to the best of your knowledge, Mladen Naletilic, did he -- was he part of those who entered and who shouldn't have entered the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mladen Naletilic, nickname Tuta, never came to the prison as himself during working hours while I was there from 8.00 to 4.00, nor did I have any knowledge or neither did I read about that in any of the reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll take note of what you said. A question from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A short question, Witness. A moment ago you said that Mr. Berislav Pusic was a member of the military police until July when he became head of the exchange office. Now, what do you mean when you say member of the military police? Was he a soldier in a uniform with a rank or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While Berislav Pusic was a member of the military police he wore a uniform just like I did. Now, as far as rank is concerned, I don't think there were any ranks. I don't think anybody had ranks at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that he wore the same uniform as you, and what was your uniform like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a camouflage uniform of the military police just like the other soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And did you have a white belt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I didn't, actually. I had a green belt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why did you have a green belt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I found it more suitable and in some -- on some occasions I wore a white belt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Mr. Pusic, what kind of belt did he have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really can't say what kind of belt he had. I didn't notice whether he had one, what it was like. It was a long time ago for me to be able to say, but all I can say is that he wore a uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you next, please, to look at Exhibit 3209. And if I can start, sir, by asking if you look at the signature portion of the document, it -- the typing on the document appears that it was prepared for the signature of Mr. Bozic, but can you confirm to us that that is your signature on the document?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us -- looking at this document, can you just say a bit more to the Judges about this particular incident, shooting incident, at the prison?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we came to work in the morning, we found out that during the night there had been some shooting at the windows of the hall and the school where the detainees were located. The deputy commander of the brigade was immediately informed about that; that was Mr. Mile Pusic. And they intervened to stop the shooting. Those were all the words of Mr. Slavko Kozul.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is one of the men that you identified, I believe, yesterday as one of the shift commanders; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Slavko Kozul.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In terms of the document itself, the distribution is to Mr. Bruno Stojic, Mr. Valentin Coric, Mr. Zvonko Vidovic, and Mr. Berislav Pusic. Now, you signed the letter. Do you recall whether you actually also prepared the letter? Maybe you originally prepared it for Mr. Bozic's signature, but in any event, do you know -- did you prepare this letter yourself and then ultimately sign it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And why did you send a copy of this report to Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The importance of the situation which occurred, luckily there weren't any casualties but there could have been. For this to be prevented, I thought that it would come to the representative of Mr. Bruno Stojic; Valentin Coric, the head; as well as Zvonko Vidovic, the head of the crime prevention department; and Mr. Berislav Pusic, from the military police administration. For them to understand the seriousness of the situation and the situation at Heliodrom, because I stress that there are few military policemen, not enough, and that it was not possible to provide security with the number of military men available. And at that time there were 16 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell the Judges, to the best of your knowledge, that is as far as you know, was anyone ever punished, disciplined or held accountable for that shooting incident around the 5th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this document testifies to the fact that between 1.00 and 3.00 a.m. on the 5th of July, 1993, unidentified soldiers shot at the windows of the school building. You yourself or Mr. Bozic, independently of the report -- well, you can't say anything about the report. It's done as it should be. But did you -- these soldiers must have belonged to a unit, and you must have given their descriptions to their superiors. So did the prison authorities take any steps with respect and contact the responsible military persons in the Heliodrom to try and understand and unravel what had actually happened, because they could have been drunken soldiers, one soldier or more soldiers who were drunk and shot. It could have been an organised incident. So it gives rise to a whole number of questions. Now, at the level of the prison authorities, did you contact the responsible military authorities of the Heliodrom compound to find out exactly what had happened?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the report that was written at that time, it was emphasised that the deputy commander of the 3rd Brigade, Mr. Mile Puzic had been informed as well as the brigade police and the military police that was in town at the mechanical engineering faculty in Mostar, and they indicated -- they reported the incident and asked them to solve it, that is to say, the brigade police and our own police to investigate the incident. However, according to what Mr. Slavko Kozul said, that was not done. So the shooting stopped of its own accord. Everything was sent out by the book as it should have been so that the deputy commander, Mr. Mile Pusic, with his brigade police force, should find the perpetrators and punish them. Whether he actually did find them and punish them, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Scott, if I'm asking a question which you would have asked. You complain here that you have not enough police force to guard the camp. Were there any consequences? Was the police force reinforced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the report you say there were 16 policemen to provide security. Now, these 16 in realtime or 16 in total? Or in a word, this number 16, is it the number of the total number of the policemen or is it a number which changed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time we had 16 military policemen, and in the report, I said that we needed -- that we would need another 16 military policemen in order to be able to provide security for the prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to this figure of 17. Now, I assume that among the 16 there are some who -- who are off at night, asleep at night. Others might be off on furlough. Others might be sick. So there are not 16 of them at all times. Now, during the night, in order to guard all these prisoners, how many military policemen were there on duty? Through the night, for example, awake, alert, in order to ensure proper security for at least three buildings, the school, the sports hall, and the other building, the prison.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to this report, the security for these four buildings, there were only 16 military policemen. That's what I'm reading here. Now, I can't say whether it was 16, 17, or 18, actually, because it was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I might --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're looking at the report, but I would like to tap into our memory. You say there were 16 to guard four buildings. Does that mean four per building or does it mean that there were a total of 16 to provide security for the whole penitentiary compound? That's what I want to know. Were there 16 at night or 16 in total for everything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were 16 policemen employed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I might assist, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you told us yesterday that there were shifts at the prison and sometimes you said there were 12-hour visits and sometimes there were 8-hour shifts. Now, to follow up on the President's question, when you say there were military policemen, are you saying that these 16 military policemen would then be spread out over the various shifts? So some would be on the nightshift, some would be on the dayshift, what have you? How many of these 16 policemen were actually guarding the facility at any one time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a small number. I know that they couldn't cover it all, so that in the building because the -- in the school building, because the school building and the sports hall were together, there were two men working, sometimes three, in one shift. Two or three on duty in one shift.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- go on. At that moment, between 1.00 and 3.00 in the night, some policemen were out on duty; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It seems, furthermore, that they did absolutely nothing, that they did not react in any way to this shooting. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the report here, all I can see is that they reported the incident to the brigade police which was put up at Heliodrom and the military police at the mechanical engineering factory, which means that they could not have stood up to this because an even bigger conflict would have flared up. That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Anyway, you say that the shooting stopped without police intervention. That means that the guards did not intervene. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what can be deduced from the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Is this the way that the service of guards was conceived at Heliodrom, that they should not intervene when anyone shot at -- at prison premises? Was that their order? Did they have that order not to react in such a case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the order is concerned itself, the work of the military policemen was to protect, to provide protection for the prisoners and not to allow forcible entry or forced entry, and not to allow disturbances of any kind, war prisoners to be disturbed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's what one assumes. Now it appears that this duty was not fulfilled. Was any disciplinary action taken against those who were on guard at that time and did not react during two hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, unless the warden might have done something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, moving on then to -- from this incident to another topic. Can you tell the Judges generally, please, whether the prisoners who were detained and brought in during this June, July 1993 time period, were they then taken out at various times from the Heliodrom to perform -- well, on various labour details?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you explain what you mean about -- of these -- what do you mean by details, duties?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Forgive me.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What duties and details?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were prisoners taken from the Heliodrom, outside of the Heliodrom to perform labour?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when do you recall first learning that in the course of being taken out to perform labour prisoners were being killed, wounded, injured, or disappearing in some way?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as wounding was concerned and injury and what happened, where they were taken, in the places where they were taken to do labour, I didn't know about that, nor did I see a single wounded or killed person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you, please, to go to P 03171.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you repeat the number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, 3171. And, sir, this appears to be a report dated the 4th of July, 1993, so quite early in this period. Again, although there is the typed named Stanko Bozic, is it in fact your signature on this report?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, please, how the information came to you for the purpose of preparing this report that two prisoners, Mr. Ramic and Mr. Cilic, had been wounded while being taken out on a labour assignment?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they were taken, pursuant to the order, the prisoners of war, they were -- when they were being taken out, they were all registered, their names and surnames, made a list of by the shift commander who let them go. And the person who took them off signed for them. And after labour was completed, and that was usually after 4.00 p.m. when we'd already gone home, those prisoners of war would come back from having performed the labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But how did you find out or how would you find out on any given occasion, in particular, this occasion, how did you find out that two of the prisoners had been wounded?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning Mr. Ante Smiljanic brought in a report to Mr. Bozic about all the things that happened during the night or, rather, everything that happened from 4.00 p.m. until the next morning. Then Mr. Smiljanic would inform Mr. Stanko Bozic, and then the secretary, Snjezana Cvitanovic, would compile the report like this one, this report, which I, on that morning, as you can see, signed for Mr. Bozic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that most of the prisoners who were taken out for labour, they would be returned to the facility after 4.00?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the first letter of the report that you signed it says: "On 3 July 1992, pursuant to written request number 01-41/93 by the 7th Battalion of the 3rd Brigade, detainees were provided for work with the approval of Mr. Berislav Pusic." Now, can you explain to the Judges, please, what role Mr. Pusic played in the approval of sending prisoner for forced labour?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Berislav, as a worker of the military police, could allow labour and allow people to go out to perform labour, and probably at that time, it was Mr. Berislav Pusic who had to be asked, because otherwise he wouldn't have -- his name wouldn't have been mentioned in this report had that not been necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why did you send your report to Mr. Coric?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was constant practice wherein we, the prison, had to report everything to the chief of the military police, the chief of the crime prevention service, Mr. Zvonko Vidovic, and Mr. Berislav Pusic, as the officer in charge of control of the military police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Judges, you touched on this a moment ago, but could you explain to the Judges your understanding of the procedure, if you will, from start to finish, in terms of an HVO unit requesting prisoners to be taken out of the Heliodrom for labour? How would such a request be made? How would it be processed to the point of the prisoners then actually leaving the facility to go out and work?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were various periods as far as the release of prisoners for labour was concerned. We, as the military prison, were not entitled to let anyone go out to do labour without an order. At the beginning, brigade commanders or battalion commanders could take them out. Military police could take prisoners out all the time because we were under the military police. But later, specific people were appointed who could issue approvals for the prisoners to go out to do labour. One of them was the commander of the town defence or, rather, the commander of the AT unit, light infantry unit, Mr. Miro [as interpreted] Jelic. So that the greatest number of exits for labour was approved by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I'll stop you for a moment please just to correct the transcript. On line 19, sir, it's been recorded -- the name you've given has been recorded as Miro, M-i-r-o, Jelic. Is that correct or could you spell it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mijo, M-i-j-o.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you've indicated that Mr. Jelic was a commander of a, what was called here in the record, of a light infantry unit. And can you tell the Judges, was that a military unit organisation of the military police?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask you please to turn in your bundle to Exhibit 2638. If you have that, sir, can you tell us, is this the type of document or order that you and people at the Heliodrom prison became familiar with as an order concerning the use of prisoners from the Heliodrom for labour? In this particular instance, dated, in fact, the 5th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when we look at the name on the bottom of this document in terms of who -- or for whose signature it was prepared, is this the Mijo Jelic that you were testifying about just a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Looking at the first part of that under the words "Order" -- under the word "Order," it says, "As of the 5th of June, 1993, the unit --" It says "1st light attack BVP is allowed to take five male prisoners from the SVIZ Heliodrom Mostar. Mr. Meho Gosto is personally responsible for taking over the prisoners for their security and welfare while they would be carrying out the public works. The prisoners are to be treated in accordance with the international humanitarian law and Geneva Conventions." Now, going back to the question I asked you a moment ago, how would the 1st light attack BVP on the 5th of June, 1993, if you know, how would that unit communicate, "Please send us five prisoners to work for us today"? How would that work?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A driver from this light assault brigade or the person who was supposed to bring the prisoners out would bring this order, enter the prison, and go to see the shift commander. And this person would show the list to the shift commander, who would then select five persons. And when the person bringing out the prisoners of war would sign the paper, the number of their military badge would be taken down. If it was a military policeman, then -- or a number of his ID, military ID if it was a soldier, and then that person would take the people out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can just pause here to inform the Chamber and, again, if we have time at the end of Mr. Praljak's testimony, we may come back to this, but in the bundle of materials, the binders and bundles of materials that have been provided to the Chamber, bundle number 3 is a set of a large number of orders for the use of detainees for labour. I don't know how many exhibits are in that bundle exactly offhand, although it goes on for -- the list itself goes on for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a question. Have you finished, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No. If I could just finish assisting the Chamber, I hope. That's bundle 3. Bundle 4 is a set of documents, requests for prisoners for labour primarily signed by a person named Puljic. Bundle number 7 is a set of documents listed in a 33-page index of approvals to take detainees for labour. Bundle 8 is a set of materials listed in 17 pages of reports concerning detainees who had been beaten, wounded, or killed who are performing forced labour. Exhibit bundle number 10 is a two-page list of various logbooks related to the taking of prisoners for forced labour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have looked at this document, just as those in the bundles 3, 4, and others. I note that there is a great number of orders saying at the end that the prisoners would be treated in keeping with the international humanitarian law, Geneva Conventions, et cetera. Now, in your mind, what did this phrase mean? What was it that prisoners were able or could do outside, and what couldn't they do in keeping with international treaties? Could you share with us your views on that issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This very phrase "treat them in keeping with international humanitarian law and the Geneva Conventions" expresses a certain attitude toward the prisoner of war, meaning that he should not be mistreated, insulted, beaten, and most importantly, that he should not be taken to places where his life would be in danger. In other words, he should be removed from the front line. As we see in every order that has been to given us, the labour is strictly specified: Cleaning streets, cleaning parks, cleaning premises. And that in itself specifies that these people would not be at risk. That is my personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have given us your explanation. Now, following from that, when you make a report saying that two detainees were injured, did you ask yourself -- as they were wounded by BH fire, doesn't that mean that they were at risk after all? When you analyse the situation, a situation where two detainees were wounded by BH fire, at the same time as telling us in line 13 that prisoners should not be exposed to risk, how does that tally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This order doesn't say that I am in a position to see them when they are taken out. The shift commander gets an order that neither I nor Stanko Bozic have access to. The shift commander is the only one who sees the order and who approves that labour. In the morning when a report is made for the previous day to Mr. Stanko Bozic, it is only then that we find out somebody was injured or wounded. I can say with full responsibility that all those things that happened, and we can see all that in the reports, were the responsibility of Mr. Stanko Bozic. He took care of that, together with two doctors from the infirmary who have generally extended assistance in such cases, and Mr. Stanko Bozic did his utmost. That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you have on the screen this text, we see in the B/C/S version that the order was written on a form where you only have to fill in the names and the dates, which means that it was a current practice to require prisoners for labour. To the best of your knowledge, how many prisoners went out each day to work in different areas, in different locations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't tell you, but many of them went out. I couldn't give you the exact number. You can see that in the reports and in the records. There is a record of how many people went out to work each day. I wouldn't like to speculate on the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Scott. If I may just continue in this direction. Mr. Praljak, was there any system to control whether the prisoners were actually employed for these innocent tasks that were indicated in the requests and whether they were really treated in accordance with international humanitarian law and the Geneva Conventions and, if so, how was this control operated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the prison is concerned, the prison was not able to know where prisoners were going. They were taken from Heliodrom to various locations, but we didn't know where.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, this is quite a surprising answer. The prisoners were in your hands, under your administration, and in your responsibility. I would suppose that a minimum would be that there is a regular control by talking to these prisoners and asking them where they were, what they had been asked to do, particularly when they had been wounded. Are you telling me that nothing of this kind was done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said a moment ago that Mr. Bozic talked to prisoners. If any of those prisoners were wounded, I never had occasion to speak to them. Mr. Bozic did that and wrote the reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm not -- I'm not claiming that you personally are responsible. When I say you or the prison, I mean the prison management there. Are you aware -- can you tell us that Mr. Bozic actually investigated and found out how the prisoners were used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't know that. I wouldn't know about Bozic, and I can't speak in his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I don't ask you to speak in his name, but did you not talk about these matters? Was it something without any interest to you that prisoners under your responsibility came not back at all or came back and were wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All that I knew I reported to Mr. Bozic; I shared with him. But as for things I didn't know, I didn't hear much from other people because I didn't speak to prisoners about such things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could have the usher's assistance, please. In the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the various bundles that have been prepared, some of them I just referred to -- or all of them I just referred to, there is Exhibit 2921, and in the interest of time, I'll just ask if the usher can put that on the ELMO, please, and the -- well, first, if you could give it to the witness. Actually, I think he has it. No, he wouldn't have it in that bundle. I'm sorry, usher. No. If you could give the witness the B/C/S version and put the English version on the ELMO, please. I'm sorry. 2921. Now, sir, this is a request to Mr. Bozic, as I understand it, dated the 24th of June, 1993, to take 20 detainees to perform engineer works on the Croatian Defence Council or HVO positions in Ricinoj street. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what is your understanding when it talks about engineering works? What does that mean to you? Or to engineer works. What kind of works?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Engineering works. Probably digging. What kind of digging, I don't know. Engineering, machines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Mr. President, the accused can see only English on the screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you look on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There it is. We can see it all now, Mr. Ibrisimovic. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us, is it correct that Ricinoj street was located on the confrontation line in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ricinoj street was the place where the prison building was, where I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And where was that location in relation to the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the town of Mostar itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And where was that in location to the confrontation line between the -- excuse me, sir. Let me finish my question to you. In relation to the confrontation line between the Muslims and the Croats as of this time period in June 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ricinoj Street is the separation line in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I can just have the usher's assistance. Just one other document on this example, please. Exhibit 3194. And again with the English on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct this is a request dated the 5th of July, 1993, for five prisoners to be taken to "build bunkers between the new bank and the grammar school"?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you have any other information you can give us on the use of the word "bunkers" other than what we might think of as common usage?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, bunker means a shelter, shelter from enemy shells and shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I direct your attention, please, to the lower part of the document, and can you tell us, does that indicate again some approval by Mr. Pusic? And whose handwriting is that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my handwriting. This was approved by Berko Pusic and taken over by Miro Bevanda against his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, how do you recall putting this handwritten information on the document? How did you receive the information that Mr. Pusic had approved the taking of these prisoners to build bunkers?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This request, we see "Subject: Request ..." was something that I called Berko Pusic about. I with read to him the request, and he would approve this part where it says what is requested, and then Mr. Miro Bevanda would take it over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The request that we see, I see it's addressed to the military prison of Heliodrom, and you are asked to give a group of five prisoners, but those could also be military prisoners, detainees of the HVO who were serving a sentence. To the best of your knowledge, when you received such requests, did it ever happen that either you or somebody else provided the HVO with their own members who were serving a sentence in your prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The request itself did not specify which prisoners we wanted, and I can't remember whether it was our own men, Croats, who went out or Muslims. All I know is that the request had to be approved by the military police administration, that is Berko Pusic, and he approved it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But if those were Croats, how would that concern Mr. Berislav Pusic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand your question correctly, it is not exactly that it was of concern, but it's that the prison was not able to let these people go out without the approval of the military police administration, in other words, Mr. Berko Pusic, and he was the one we called most often whenever we needed something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, you have some time ago said that there was a certain separation of categories of prisoners; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the date that we see here, the 5th of July, I think you didn't understand me quite, Your Honour. People were separated into categories only in September, in the end of September, and there was one category only that was separated earlier, military detainees as opposed to prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Would you then say that there were in the same premises Croat and Muslim prisoners held together undistinct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were in the same building, the building of the prison, but they were physically separated so that they could not be in contact, these two groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So you should be able to tell and you must have noticed whether the orders to take out prisoners were handed to the department chief of the Croat section or a Muslim section.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat that question and make it more simple?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You have told us that the order to take out prisoners or to hand out prisoners were brought by a driver and were then handed to a shift commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You didn't understand me. When the order to release the prisoners of war came, the commander of the shift, shift commander, would select the people being asked for. He makes a list of their names into a book. He writes their names and surnames into the book saying which prisoners of war were leaving, and then at the end of that list, he signs his name. And the person who comes to collect the people signs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I did understand it that way, Mr. Praljak. I did understand that all right. My question is: Was the same shift commander in charge of Croat and of non-Croat prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. The shift commander was superior to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And have you ever witnessed -- can you tell us that a shift commander ever selected a Croat prisoner to go out to do work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not a witness to have seen that. However, I know that it was mostly the units within the Heliodrom compound who for the tasks they performed or labour would also take out Croatian detainees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: How do you know this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the words. And I saw people taken out and working in the compound, in the barracks, the building next to us, the Bojna Busic regiment, and then they would pass right underneath my window where my office was and go into the next-door building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Was that the kind of assignment we have been talking about now where Mr. Pusic would give an agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That permission wasn't issued by Mr. Pusic. It was issued by the commander of the brigade at the time, and that was Mr. Bozo Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'm sorry for interrupting you, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, it's time for the break. We're going to take a 20-minute break, and the registrar tells me that you have used almost three hours and 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, before we move forward, if we can still have -- if we can still have 2921 in front of you and the English version on the ELMO. Looking at the original language version, again below the signature line for Mr. Puljic there is some handwritten information. Can you tell us if you recognise the handwriting on the -- on that portion of the document?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whose handwriting it is, but it was written pursuant to a telephone conversation with Berko Pusic and Goran Vidovic. Twenty detainees to be given out, and they were taken over by Mr. Dragan Kozul with his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can recall and assist us. Would the communication take place with Mr. Pusic to approve it? Is that something that the local commander did or something that someone at the Heliodrom did? Can you assist us further on that.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain what's in front of me, that subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I think -- go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sent to Mr. Bozic personally, and the request came from -- or, rather, it came to the prison. The shift commander took in this request and then called Mr. Berko Pusic on the phone, and he talked to him -- or, rather, as it says here, Vidovic talked to him. Goran Vidovic talked to him. So on the basis of the conversation with Berko Pusic, these prisoners of war were given over to this unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I take it from what you told us yesterday, the only -- excuse me. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Now, I'm not clear in the transcript. Did the witness talk to Mr. Pusic or is he -- I understood it that the witness didn't speak to Mr. Pusic about this subject, but I'm not quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott. Would you clear that up? I had the impression that it was the head -- or, rather, the shift commander that telephoned Pusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I never suggested otherwise. I asked if the witness could explain to us the process by which this was done on a daily -- virtually a daily basis. Let me follow up with this question which may assist -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I do not see this so clearly and I agree with Mr. Ibrisimovic that it is unclear because it says telephone call by Berko Pusic to Goran Vidovic. So at this point we have an initiative that comes from the accused, Pusic, and then it goes to Vidovic, and from Vidovic probably it goes to prison. Now, the shift commander, we do not know what he did. Did he call Pusic, or did he call Vidovic? Who in turn called Pusic? Do you have any idea, Witness, of how this went?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On duty at the time was Mr. Goran Vidovic, who talked to Mr. Berko Pusic, and with his own hand, probably when he was on duty, wrote what it says here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So Goran Vidovic was a shift commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whether he was a shift commander or whether he worked in the shift or on the shift, I can't say for sure, but he was doing shift duty at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And following up on yesterday, sir, can you confirm to us that the only telephone that would -- at the prison that would be available for these communications was the telephone belonging to the secretary in the administration building where you and Mr. Bozic were located?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the prison building, because it was working 24 hours, round the clock, had communication with the outside exit through the switchboard of the 3rd Brigade of the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Could I ask you, please -- for the Witness to next be shown, please, Exhibit P 05457. And this is a separate bundle, Your Honour, because it's a large document. It is called on the binder -- it is binder number 15 in the overall set, and then further, bundle 13, part 3. And it's all one exhibit, the English translation and original of one exhibit, which is -- Exhibit number is P 05457.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Witness, before you look at this next document, I was thinking about what you just said regarding that telephone conversation. When I was young, I worked on a switchboard, military switchboard, so I know how these things work. Now, I seem to have the impression that you were saying that from this office one would have to go through the switchboard of the 3rd Brigade in order to get an outside connection. Does that mean that the telephone did not have direct access outside, that you would have to go through the switchboard of the 3rd Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Now, let's imagine that somebody was calling you from outside and wanted to speak to you. They would have to go through the switchboard of the 3rd Brigade, and then they would put the call through to you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We had a direct line in the administration, a separate number that didn't have to go through the brigade switchboard. There was a direct line to the secretary in her office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And why was it that when Mr. Pusic was calling, or the other way round, you had to go through the switchboard? Why couldn't you do this through the direct connection line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was used -- this line was used by myself, Bozic, and the secretary, this direct line, whereas during the night, we used the brigade switchboard because we weren't working at the time. So the prison building was connected with that switchboard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That's very precise, and it's provided me with the information I needed. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you could look now, if you have in front of you, please, if you can go to the original language version of the document which should probably be about halfway through the binder that you have in front of you. And if the Judges have the binder, for this initial purpose, you may also wish to look momentarily at least at the B/C/S version. Do you have that, sir? When you look at that binder, first of all, can you tell us what this document is, this rather lengthy document we're looking at? And if you actually go back from the first -- not the first text pages but the actual something that looks like the outside cover, which I'm told is at page 5 -- in e-court, page 5 of B/C/S and page 3 in English. On the very front -- very, very first page of the document I see something which appears to have the writing Zatvor on it. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The prison building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And there also appears to be under that, and it's not terribly legible, but one can make out what appears to be a range of dates which might be the dates that this particular journal or ledger covers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me go back to my original question. Can you tell the Judges what this document is?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is a book, a ledger, which was kept by the commanders, the shift commanders, a logbook, when orders came in for taking out prisoners for labour. When that came about, they would write the name and surname of each and every person who was to leave the premises to perform labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can then ask you -- at some points, Mr. Praljak, I may push you on a bit further because our time becomes limited. If you turn to the third or fourth page of the original language document, I believe it would be -- by counting the first pages, it would be the fifth page, you come to a page that has the word, and excuse me if I don't pronounce it correctly, but "Naputak" on the front, on the top of it. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And first of all, is that your signature on the bottom right corner?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is my signature. It's not my handwriting in the set of instructions above but it is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, with that in mind, then, can you tell us then what is written above that over your signature? What is this material or this language about? Now we can go -- for those working in English, we can go back to the translation. Of course you can see the text.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a set of instructions which quite -- was visibly put up so that every military policeman and shift commander could see it and could abide by the instructions set out when they handed over prisoners for labour. It sets out very precisely, point by point, what the instructions are and how the process should be conducted. At the end, it says that the shift commander is responsible for keeping due records and the way in which the logbook was to be handed over from one shift to another. That had to be done in the presence of the shift commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if we can move forward to the first set of actual entries in the journal and, again in the translation, I think the first one -- the first date of this particular journal is the 21st of August, 1993. Could I ask you, please, looking down to a place where it says "7th Battalion." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you just take us through this entry and tell us what this -- the information that's indicated here? For instance, under 7th Battalion it says "At 0600 hours." So what is the reference to 0600? What does that indicate to you as a record of the prison?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people listed below went out early in the morning, at 6.00 a.m., pursuant to the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you can tell by looking at this that there were 20 individuals who went out?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the name of the person who actually received, took custody, if you will, of these people when they were taken out of the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: After these 20 people, it says that Miro Lovric took them out. Since he didn't have a military ID card, his personal ID number was recorded along with his signature, and underneath the signature it says that they returned from having performed labour at 2040 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just to pick up on various --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 2045 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just to pick up on various questions that have been asked in the course of the last two days about time. Is it fair to say, then, this would be an example of prisoners who left at 6.00 in the morning before you and Mr. Bozic and the administrative building were operating, and they were brought back at 8.45 in the evening after -- again, after you and Mr. Bozic would have left the premises? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, everyone can see that this goes on for some number of pages, and we're not going to -- unless the Chamber has additional questions, we're not going to go through, of course, the many entries because of the time. Sir, is it correct that this particular journal is for -- when it says Zatvor on the front, this is the journal or logbook for the prison building itself? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the book that they kept and made entries in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, can I ask you, please, to next be shown a similar bundle exhibit which is 4360 -- P 04367?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Which, Your Honours, and for the courtroom, is in binder 14 of the total set of binders, and also marked for further as bundle 13, part 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if you can turn quickly, sir, to again the -- approximately the middle of that stack of material until you find the original language version, and the very front page, the exterior front page, if you will. Does that say on the front of it "Skola" and "Hale"?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I might be allowed in the interests of time, is this essentially an identical journal, in fact, including the same page of instructions signed by you, but this was the journal that was maintained for those prisoners who were taken out of either the school or the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the format of the entries would be the same as those that we were just looking at; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just before we leave this, then, to follow up on earlier questions from the Chamber and in particular Judge Trechsel, is it correct again to recall that in the school and in the sports hall only prisoners of war were kept? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And could I next ask you, please, to look at -- in the -- returning to the principal working bundle of exhibits, Exhibit 4871.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, may I -- may I remain with this document for another question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, if you look at the page numbers up to the right, and if you look at page 01535046, which is an example. There are move. You have a number of names with a circle around them. Can you explain what this circle means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really can't answer that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm astonished, Mr. Praljak. You gave out directions as to how this logbook was to be kept. Now, there is a sign which is really clearly visible, and you say you do not know what it means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the end of this -- it's just now that I've read it. It says that Mate Kozul, and the number of the badge that he returned, that 10 detainees remained out doing labour who were circled, which means that these 10 individuals with the circles round their names were not returned, and that was in the morning. The shift commander, in his report, is reporting to Stanko Bozic, and on the basis of this, the report was compiled about these people who were not returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Where would that report be, Mr. Praljak? In -- somewhere else. The report has no traces in this document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, but the person who writes this says they remain outside when they were taken to perform labour. Ten individuals, that 10 individuals were not returned and that Mr. Bozic knew about this, and most probably he wrote a letter about what happened to those people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak. Mr. Praljak, did you or did anybody else regularly check on this logbook, control whether it was correct and what the entries were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It had to be correct, because for taking over the people and the exactness of the information here, you have the signature of the person who took the people out and therefore who was responsible for those people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: This was not my question, Mr. Praljak. I asked you whether you or someone else regularly looked up this logbook and checked what was happening, what the entries were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As to the reports that were written, Mr. Bozic would receive a report from Ante Smiljanic every morning which ought to be correct, should have been correct. And then Mr. Bozic knew about its correctness, because in -- if the people were not there, then the people that Mr. Bozic had a list of who had not returned would ask that all these people be returned. He would do this through the SIS employees. That is to say, that certain people who had not been returned be returned, because then he didn't know where they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You have still not answered my question, Mr. Praljak. It is a very simple question. Did you or to your knowledge someone else regularly look at this logbook and check what the entries were, or were they left with the shift commanders and the management of the prison just didn't bother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The shift commander was responsible to the warden for security. Now, Ante Smiljanic who had an insight --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak. Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I am asking you whether you or, to your knowledge, someone else regularly controlled this logbook. The answer is yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. Who did? Did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In most cases it was Mr. Ante Smiljanic, Stanko Bozic, and from time to time I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just a point of clarification, Your Honours, based on the questions that you've just asked, Judge Trechsel. The instructions were signed by the gentleman as the warden, the instructions that you were referring to, and it would seem to me that based on that, this gentleman was acting as the warden at least with respect to the instructions, and therefore the shift commanders would have been directly his subordinates. Might -- in line of your questioning, might you wish to inquire of that, because it might be important later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you for the suggestion. You have heard, Mr. Praljak, what Mr. Karnavas, counsel for Mr. Prlic, has just said. You signed the instructions as warden. Were the shift commanders responsible to you or to Mr. Bozic or to both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you can see, throughout 1993, I signed in different ways. I signed this at a moment in time when Mr. Cvitkovic from the military police administration department, Franjo Cvitkovic was his name, told me that greater security, tighter security should be implemented. On that same day he told me that I should compile this form, and when this tighter security was implemented -- I think it was in place for a short time, because I was issued a subsequent order from Mr. Bruno Stojic as the fifth member for introducing more law and order into the prison. So during that short space of time, Ante Smiljanic once again, in the post that he was, and he remained security commander, and Stanko Bozic was never replaced as the warden and commander of the prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder whether this is entirely clear, but I would leave it for cross-examination, because I do not want to abuse too much of Mr. Scott's kind patience. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In -- in partial response to your question, Judge Trechsel, and to the Chamber in general, again, I would just highlight for the purposes of the record and to advise the Chamber, there is also a set of materials called bundle number 8 which have a separate table. All the bundles have a separate schedule or table in front. Bundle number 8 lists 120 separate exhibits which are all reports about detainees being beaten, wounded, or killed. And there's 120 exhibits starting with the first Exhibit number being 03171 and continuing on to Exhibit 8147. And in those 120 separate exhibits, all of those contain information about prisoners taken for forced labour who were either beaten, wounded, or killed. And as one example of that, if I can ask again for the assistance of the usher.
