If you can put the English version on the ELMO and show the witness the -- and this is Exhibit P 03435, which again is part of bundle 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And first of all, sir, if we can look -- if you look at the original language version once again. Even though it has the typed name of Mr. Bozic, is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the signature of Mr. Bozic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. I'm sorry. I don't have it immediately in front of me, and I can't see the B/C/S version at the moment. My apology. Is this a form that you are familiar with again, that you can tell the Chamber that this is the type of report that you saw being prepared around this time, this one being specifically for an event on the 10th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This kind of report. I think Bozic did the contact -- contacts and wrote 99 per cent of these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This again is a record of in general -- more generally of a -- the taking of 30 detainees based on an order signed by Mijo Jelic, handed over for work with the permission of military police control officer Berislav Pusic, given over to a military policeman by the name of Baresic, badge number 3233, and one of the detainees was wounded in the leg by the BH army and taken to the hospital for treatment. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm lost. I don't know what documents you're using. We have two bundle 8. We have part of it in binder 7, and then we have part in binder 8, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If you'll allow me to -- I'm advised that it's in binder 7. It was in the complete set. It might not be the subset that was provided to each Judge. I think it's -- it's Exhibit P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I just before that -- could I assist. It is Exhibit P 03435, the English version of which is on the ELMO now, because I understood that finding the binders might be a problem is the reason I put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I've got it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry. And the witness has the B/C/S version in front of him. And I believe it's also in e-court at the moment as far as I can see it. No? I can't tell. Is it on e-court as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. My question goes in this direction precisely. Mr. Scott is questioning now on the form of the document. I think it would have been more logical to ask the witness if he knows about the event itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll continue on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir -- unless I've misread the document, I think I've accurately read it. Can I just ask you, sir, again why this kind of report then -- is it true that this standard type of report then would also be communicated on to Mr. Coric, Mr. Pusic, and Mr. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I take it -- is it correct, sir, that when we went through the bundle of 120 separate exhibits, they would all basically look pretty much like this, the ones you were able to look at over the weekend?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So as a result this one particular document, in response to various lines of inquiry from the Chamber, in particular Judge Trechsel, certainly Mr. Bozic, on preparing this report, was aware that this prisoner had been wounded in the leg, and at least according to this record, that information had been sent on to Mr. Coric, Mr. Pusic, and Mr. Vidovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could, finally on this topic, ask you then to -- going back to the principal working bundle, Exhibit P 04871. Do you have that, sir? This is to cover again for the Judges to see as many different types of records and forms as possible. Can you tell us what this document is and if this was again another type of form used for the purposes of taking prisoners for labour?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a form developed by the 3rd Brigade located in Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The top of that -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And mostly these were signed by commander Bozo Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And on the top of that -- top part of that page, is it correct -- do I understand correctly, for work location and the number of prisoners, this would indicate that 25 prisoners were needed to work at Hum hill?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It indicates they were taken away on the 8th of September at 1900 hours. Can you tell -- if you can tell us anywhere on the document where it would indicate when they were returned?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's probably in the logbook that exists in the building from which they were taken, such as the one that we've seen before. It must be written when they were supposed to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to move away for the time being from the topic of forced labour, but I want the Chamber to understand that I intend to come back to that topic. We're not leaving the topic permanently, but I will come back to it in a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, moving to a different topic, in the course of 1993, did you come to know of a practice by which prisoners at the Heliodrom prison could be released from the custody of the prison in order to go to a third country or to the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you very briefly, please -- can you, please, explain your understanding on how that procedure worked. What did a prisoner have to do to get himself or herself released to go to a third country?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somebody would come from the office for exchanges. Mostly it was Jerko Radic or Tomo Sakota. They would bring a certificate, as I described before. And now I can only add briefly that the signature would read Berislav Pusic with the approval of a SIS officer, and Miro Music, and an officer of the crime prevention service, Vidovic. Jerko or Tomo Sakota who would come on that occasion, on such occasions, would have a paper, a letter of guarantee that somebody would receive them in a third country. They would come bringing that kind of paper and take the person concerned, who would then leave the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, please, whether this practice, that is the release of prisoners to a third country, is that something that came about after the arrest starting on the 30th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The certificate itself and the method of release is the same. It's just that somebody from the family or a friend had to bring the certificate to the prisoner and the prison so that the request be approved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. But just -- my question was more specifically when this practice started and whether you can confirm that that was the practice, that is releasing prisoners to third countries based on this procedure, when that practice first came into existence and went forward.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when we had the greatest number of those prisoners of war, starting with July, that's when most of them were released on the basis of these letters of guarantee.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask you to look at Exhibit P 04686 in the main bundle, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 04686. P 04686. Sir, can you confirm that this is the record concerning the release of someone by the first name of Zijo around the 31st of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is that the type of paperwork or form that you are familiar with that was used for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to look next at 06436. And can you tell us what that Exhibit 6436 is?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was made by Mr. Bozic, and it's a list of detainees who were held at the prison and had a letter of guarantee. It was sent to Mr. Berislav Pusic in person, that is, to the office for exchange. Based on this document and those letters of guarantee, a team of people would release these people against the signature of Mr. Berislav Pusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And a similar document - excuse me - number 6816. Is that a similar record, same format but on -- dated the 22nd of November, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, what was the purpose of sending this information to Mr. Pusic, if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could explain. Because all these people who were in prison and who received such letters of guarantee, in order to be released, needed the signature of Mr. Berislav Pusic from the office of exchange. For that reason and according to the records that were kept and the office of exchange or the ICRC or whoever, would send this paper to him so that he could do this part of the work with the crime prevention service or the SIS before he gives his approval to release these people, and after getting that approval, Mr. Berko Pusic would have them released.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honours, unless you have questions on that, I'm going to move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, so you've just told us that one of the ways to leave the Heliodrom or to leave Herceg-Bosna for a third country was to have this letter of guarantee to go to a third country. Did you ever learn about a particular political party coming into the Heliodrom for purposes of meeting with the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us about that, please?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 30th of June, when people started to be brought in in large groups, maybe a day or two passed, not more, before a group of people came to Heliodrom to see Mr. Bozic. Those were a party of Mr. Pohara. I don't know if I will get the name right, but I think it was MDS, and his members from the town of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did MDS, to your knowledge, stand for the Muslim Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't give it much thought, but I would probably translate it as you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you said these representatives of this MDS party associated with Mr. Pohara came and met with Mr. Bozic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I was there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what was that discussion about? What did this party want to do?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The objective of this party was to hold a meeting with a group of Muslim detainees from all the various buildings where they were held. The reason was they wanted to tell them that all those who accept the platform of that party can leave the prison immediately and return to their homes where they, the party, would take care of them. That was the point of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I ask you this next question, Mr. Praljak, not -- I think I know your answer, but because I expect the Judges would ask it if I didn't. Do you know what the politics or platform of this particular party was?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know, because I did not belong to that party, and I know nothing about their platform or their objectives. It's the first time I've heard of them then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I -- before continuing on with this, when these people came and met with you and Mr. Bozic, presumably in the administrative building, to ask if they could talk to the Muslim prisoners about this, did Mr. Bozic have authority on his own to allow a political party to come into the prison for the purposes of a meeting with prisoners, or to your understanding, would that have required the authorisation of somebody else?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody, including a political -- a political party could go into the barracks or the perimeter of the prison without approval. That means that Mr. Bozic must have had approval from somebody that they should be allowed in. I didn't see that approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I take it from your answer you can't provide us any more particulars as to who gave the approval above Mr. Bozic's level for the purpose of this political party to come into the prison?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did, in fact, as a result of this meeting with Mr. Bozic and yourself, was this party allowed to meet with various Muslim prisoners at the facility?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us whether any Muslim prisoners actually joined the party and, as a result of joining the party, were in fact released from prison?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know the number, but not many people signed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you briefly, please, to turn to Exhibit P 03193 in your bundle. 3193. If you have that, sir, can I just direct your attention to the second paragraph of that document, the document itself being dated the 5th of July, 1993. Does that indicate that at the request of the MDS and, as previously agreed, 14 individuals, members of this party, have been released? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And would that generally be consistent with what you've told us about a few moments ago?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the interest of time, I'm not going to go to it, but I'll simply refer in the record there's a further reference to the MDS being at the prison in Exhibit P 03942. Perhaps that can be the subject of a follow-up motion on Exhibits P 03942.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Scott, it is also of some interest to note that in the same document it is said that 24 HVO members have been released.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may, sticking with this document, Your Honour. It doesn't appear, at least on the document itself, that these people that were released were converted to this particular party or joined this particular party. So -- at least at this moment. It could have been that they were already members of that party, I don't know. I'm not suggesting they were one way or the other. But, at least, based on what Mr. Scott said in his question, which seems to be assuming a fact that's not quite in evidence, at least not based on this document itself, so I am objecting to the form of the question and to the conclusion which he's trying to derive from the introduction of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm let the evidence of the witness combined with the document speak for itself. The witness indicated that he saw a few people took up the offer and were in fact released, and I think the Chamber can take that evidence and this document together and give it the value that the Chamber will decide to give.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us, please, did you find out sometime in early August 1993 that you had been appointed to a commission concerning HVO prisons, that appointment coming from Bruno Stojic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what you know about the establishment of that commission, when and how it came about? And let me just say particularly by early -- let me back up. My apology. Let me rephrase it. During late July -- during July and the first part of August of 1993, had you and Mr. Bozic been raising a number of issues and concerns about the HVO prisons, about forced labour and a number of issues, many of which -- some of which we will see in a few minutes, but can you just confirm that was the case?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you then tell us what your understanding was of the -- how the commission appointed by Mr. Stojic came into existence, as you understand it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, as the fifth member, was handed the order, and at the same time, it was brought to the awareness of Mr. Bozic as the warden. I called as soon as I received it. I saw that Mr. Berislav Pusic was the president of the commission, so I called him straight away and asked him the same day whether he had received it before me, and when I told him about the order, that I was the fifth member and when we would start working, he had nothing to tell me. He just said, "We will do the work," and that was all the answer that he gave me pursuant to this order that had been received.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before we go further on that, can I, in fact, ask you to look at Exhibit P 03942, which in fact is the very exhibit that I had indicated we would skip over, but in the very same exhibit is other information for this purpose. So if we can, in fact, look at 3942. If you have that, sir, can you confirm that this is a report from Mr. Stanko Bozic to Valentin Coric and Mijo Jelic dated the 4th of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, on the first page, since -- since we now have it in front us, on the second paragraph and in the original language version, you can see the paragraph reference if you look at the time and dates numerically dated 13.07.1993. Do you see there that in fact is a reference to that on the 13th of July, 1993, with the permission of Mr. Vidovic, the MDS was able to talk with members at the Heliodrom? The Heliodrom being the facility that Mr. Bozic is reporting about? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, can you look at the document, please, more generally and can you just tell the -- again, our time is unfortunately short. In the course of this report, does Mr. Bozic raise with Mr. Coric and Mr. Jelic a number of issues or concerns about matters at the Heliodrom as of early August 1993?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This report was written on the 30th of June -- or, rather, from the 30th of June to the 4th of August. It relates to that entire period.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Does it indicate, for example, a number of health issues including people -- detainees having scabs? Does it talk about security lapses?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is there anything written in this report by Mr. Bozic that you disagree with or that you don't confirm as being a concern that the two of you had at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd have to read through it but that would take time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There's a paragraph, sir, toward -- toward the latter part of the document. It says: "Every day we encounter security lapses." If you can find that. "Although we warned in reports numbered 506/93 and 516/93 that detainees were being taken home by our soldiers. Nothing has been undertaken to stop this. To date nine detainees have been wounded by the BH army while working." Do you see that passage?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you have any information whether either you or Mr. Bozic received any response from Mr. Coric or Mr. Jelic to this report?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. I don't know if Mr. Bozic did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This report is dated the 4th of August, 1993, and then in reference to what we were talking about a few moments ago, if I can please ask you now to return to P 03995. And, sir, is that the order by Bruno Stojic dated four days later, on the 8th of August, 1993, establishing the commission of which you were a member?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And are you listed as the fifth person appointed to this commission, the first person listed being Mr. Berislav Pusic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who did you understand or come to know to be the president of this commission established by Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Berislav Pusic, as it says in the order itself, next to his name, is the president of the office for exchanges and president of the commission. The last word says "President."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's -- your previous testimony has left the screen that most of us have in front us now, Mr. Praljak, but I believe you said some minutes ago now that when you learned of your appointment you had a short conversation with Mr. Pusic? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What did you say to him and what did he say to you in response?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as I received it and saw his name there - Mr. Bozic was with me - I rang up straight away. The conversation was not long. All I told him was that I received the order and that I was a member, and I asked him when are we going to work. He never said when. He just said, "We'll do the work." Perhaps he hadn't actually received this order at the time that I rang him up. I can't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: After that conversation with Mr. Pusic, could you tell the Judges, did you ever hear from Mr. Pusic again about the work of this commission?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you ever attend a meeting of this commission?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Before that I should have asked, were you ever invited or given notice of any meetings of this commission?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you at any time report to the person who established this commission, Mr. Stojic? Did you ever communicate to Mr. Stojic, to your knowledge, the commission had never in fact been made operational? To your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you recall approximately when that was that you communicated that to Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a document, but I wrote it to be handed personally to Mr. Bruno Stojic and to Mr. Mladen Naletilic, aka Tuta. And after that I wrote again. I wrote another letter which was addressed to General Roso, Mr. Perica Jukic, and others who were named in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just on those points, sir, at the time that those -- that second letter was written, the one you just referred to, by approximately November of 1993, had Mr. Slobodan Praljak been replaced as top commander or head commander of the HVO by Mr. Roso, and had Mr. Stojic been replaced as minister of defence by Mr. Perica Jukic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time I didn't know that, so that's how I wrote the report. All I did know was that General Roso had arrived and that he was occupying that position. As for Mr. Bruno Stojic, I didn't know that he had been replaced because I addressed the letter to him. And then I was told that he had been replaced by Perica Jukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I next ask you to look at Exhibit P 04002. And if you have that, sir -- if you can just look at that for a moment. There's actual two documents that are almost the same, or perhaps they are the same, but in the interest of time, could you also then look at P 04141. Both of those documents, sir, appear to be a record or purport to be a record of action by the commission established by Mr. Stojic for action taken on the 12th of August. Excuse me. And the second of the two documents, if we could just look at that one, 4141, on the 12th of August, 1993. And could you just start by telling us, you're listed at the end of this document, I believe you're -- give me a moment, please. In the earlier handwritten version which is the 4002, 4002, you are listed -- someone has listed your name in handwriting, Josip Praljak. Can you simply tell us, did you in fact ever attend a meeting of this commission on the 12th of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And until -- until you saw this document in the last several days, were you ever aware that the commission had issued such a document or taken such an action around that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In paragraph number 1 of what's called a decision, and I'm now going to be referring to 4141, again it talks about the issue of classification. And can you tell the Judges, Mr. Praljak, as of the 12th of August, 1993, as to the prisoners who were kept at the Heliodrom, what was their status of classification or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the prisoners of war are concerned, up until the 12th of August they were not separated. The prisoners of war were not separated from the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did -- did you know, did the prison management know, or if you know, did anyone in the HVO, of the people that were being held at the Heliodrom, did anyone know which ones were prisoners of war and which ones were civilians?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the service who worked, led by Zvonko Vidovic, knew that, and the SIS, those who had their particulars and documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention next to Exhibit P 4352.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you repeat the number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. P 04352. Sir, this is a report to Mr. Bruno Stojic dated the 20th of August, 1993, which I believe the Chamber has seen previously. Is it correct that in this letter Mr. Bozic raises three numbered concerns here, one, sending detainees to work; two, the quality and quantity of food; three, bad conditions in solitary cells? And did Mr. Bozic communicate to Mr. Stojic at this time that he was concerned about violations of the Geneva Conventions and possibly being brought before an international Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall whether either you, Mr. Praljak or Mr. Bozic, received any response from Mr. Stojic to the report dated the 20 August 1983?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me just for the record, so the record is clear, what was just put in the transcript, sir, is, "I don't know about him." I asked you whether you or Mr. Bozic received any response to Mr. Bozic's report to Mr. Stojic. Are you aware of any response that either you or Mr. Bozic received?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. Whether Mr. Bozic did receive any, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you please to look at Exhibit 4512. This is a report dated the 25th of August, 1993, apparently prepared, it appears to be, for Mr. Bozic's signature, but is that in fact your signature?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell the Judges, without looking at every single such document, were you continuing to report about the wounding of prisoners taken for forced labour during this time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is that particular document, 4512, would you consider that to be representative of the type of reports that you and Mr. Bozic were making during this time period?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask you next to please look at Exhibit 4500. 4500. Is that a report, sir, dated the 25th of August, 1993, that you sent to the office for the exchange of captives, attention Mr. Berko Pusic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct that this concerned a list of detainees who had come from Doljani and Sovici and at least three of whom, number 15, 16, and 17, were receiving medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why did you send this particular report or others like it to Mr. Pusic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the representative of the office for exchange, he had to have all the information about every detainee who was in prison, and here we have a list of detainees from Doljani and Sovici who were at that time doing labour or were in hospital for treatment on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us around this time, August of 1993, because I'm not sure the Chamber will know the name or not -- if you do, Your Honours, I apologise for taking your time. But, sir, can you tell us who Zarko Tole was and what position he held in August of 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that he was a general. Now, what post he held and what task he performed, I don't know. All I know is that he was at the headquarters in Citluk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say headquarters, headquarters of what?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you know that Mr. Tole to be the Chief of Staff, head of administration, if you will, chief of administration to either Mr. Slobodan Praljak or Mr. Petkovic or both?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know what his duties were. All I did know was that he was in Citluk and that that's where his headquarters were, but what function he exercised, I don't know. He was a general. A general's a general.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd ask you to look at Exhibit 4233. 4233. Sir, according to this document, which is dated the 16th of August, 1993, it appears to bear your signature, if you can confirm that. You wrote a letter or made a report to Mr. Zarko Tole. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, let me go back, sir. Surely in writing a letter to someone you've indicated as a senior officer, you must have had some information as to why you would take the time to bother to write a letter to Mr. Tole around the middle of August 1993, as to who he was and why it might be important for him to receive such a letter.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a lot of time had passed and on the report here, which is correct as it was, as it was written, it said the Main Staff -- it was addressed to the Main Staff, and Mr. Zarko Tole was probably the head of the Main Staff of the HVO. But I didn't know that level of command because it was a higher level that I wasn't acquainted with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was Mr. Tole -- and I realise, Your Honour, we're coming up on a break, if I can have just one or two more questions about this document. Was Mr. Tole in your immediate chain of command, sir? If you can tell us that.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my opinion, no, he wasn't. But I did address him because I addressed all the others, too, who were above superior, that something should be done. I addressed them as a member of the commission, and I addressed him too so that he should be informed of the situation as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: By the middle of August and even by the end of August, sir, can you tell the Judges whether you had received any satisfaction from either Mr. Stojic, Mr. Coric, Mr. Pusic, or anyone else to whom you were making your various complaints?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, it might be time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we did not see that Mr. Praljak sent any complaints to Mr. Pusic as the president of the commission, so I object to that question from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll come back to it if Your Honours want me to after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He should -- he should describe under what -- exactly what his position is under the signature or above the signature. It says that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'll do that. I'll ask. We'll save time. Mr. Praljak, when you signed, you were assistant commander of the 5th Battalion of the military police, were you? And underneath it says "Deputy warden." Do you confirm that you were indeed attached to the 5th Battalion of the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the whole of the prison was part of the 5th Battalion of the military police from June 1993 onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And within the 5th Battalion, did you have a rank or position of assistant commander? Assistant battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So why then does it say that under your name or above your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that, but I was the deputy warden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So does that mean that you signed anything and everything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not anything and everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you said, I don't know. Your answer was, I don't know. Now, you're given a title here and you're signing under that title. So are you challenging the fact that you were assistant commander of the 5th Battalion assistant to or just assistant commander, whatever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I never was any of that. I was never the assistant commander of the 5th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the gentleman indicated on page 66, line 2 that he signed it as a member of the commission, thereby giving the implication that it was he, as a member of the commission, signing it. That question needs to be posed. We could do that after the break, but certainly from the document, there is no indication that he's sending it on behalf of him being a member of the commission, but rather as a deputy warden. And I think that was the point of the objection because the gentleman obviously is being economical with the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The observation made by Mr. Karnavas is highly relevant. When you signed this document, did you say you were signing it like -- you said you were signing it as a member of the commission, but on this document, at no point does it say that you are a member of the commission, and you're not sending a copy to the other members of the commission. So do you have an explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the fifth member of the commission, I wrote --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Don't say "as." The document doesn't mention at any point that you were a member of the commission. Perhaps in your mind you were, but this -- in this document, there's nothing which allows us to say and conclude that you were a member of the commission, and you didn't even send a copy to Mr. Pusic, did you? Well, you can think about it during the break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can answer straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Think about it. It's 12.30, and we'll reconvene in 20 minutes' time and hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, we have just a short hour ahead of us, so let's start.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, just to follow up on some questions from the Judges before the break. When you learned that you had been appointed to this commission as a result of the order by Mr. Stojic in August, did you take that seriously?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you -- did you take that to add to the responsibility that you already felt about dealing with these -- the issues that you've been telling us about yesterday and today?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So whether you said it on this document -- on a particular document or not, you felt that you were acting -- during this time period after the 11th of August, you felt that in addition to acting in your capacity as deputy warden that you also had this additional further responsibility of being a member of the Stojic commission? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to look at Exhibit 5437. And in the interest of time, sir, the point really in showing this document to you and to the Judges is, did you continue on throughout this period, continuing until even here, the 28th of September and thereafter, to make various reports and state the concerns that you had about the treatment of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is that your signature on that report?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you find around this time that not only were prisoners being taken out for labour but in many instances they were being kept out -- kept away from the Heliodrom for extended periods of time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you to, please, go to Exhibit 5881. Do you have that, sir? This appears to be an order issued by Milivoj Petkovic dated the 14th of October, 1993, from Citluk HVO headquarters indicating: "1. "I hereby prohibit the use of prisoners to carry out any type of work in the brigade zones of responsibilities. "2. If, however, this sort of activity is allowed, the permit shall be issued by the HVO Main Staff. "3. Anyone caught breaching this order shall be held accountable." Can you tell us if you recall when you first learned of this order by Mr. Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about it for the first time upon my return from sick leave somewhere towards the end of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know whether -- can you tell the Judges, did the use of forced labour continue after Mr. Petkovic issued the order reflected in this exhibit, 5881?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us about a particular instance where forced labour was -- prisoners were taken out for labour by someone named Sopta.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the word goes, Sopta, that was the commander of the 2nd brigade, Guards Brigade, which was established towards the end of 1993, and Baja Sopta didn't take them away, but it was with his signature that people left to do labour. Not only along with his signature but also that of Mile Pusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you raise the fact that these prisoners were being sent out? Did you raise that with Mr. Bozic, Stanko Bozic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I wrote a report, too, or reports to Mr. Bruno Stojic, since I didn't know that at the time he had left to take up another function elsewhere; and to General Roso; to Rado Lavric, who was acting chief of the military police administration; and Mr. Perica Jukic, who was there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, just to follow up on that. You've just mentioned the name of a man named Rado Lavric who we've -- we've seen the name on several documents. Did you learn around this time that he had become, that is late October into November 1993, in that time period, that he had become the acting chief of the HVO military police taking Mr. Coric's place?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So did you come to know again, sir, that by early November 1993 Mr. Slobodan Praljak was no longer head of the HVO, Mr. Bruno Stojic was no longer minister of defence, and Mr. Coric was no longer chief of military police?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When did you first begin to learn that information?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I sent out a report which related to -- or, rather, which was addressed to Mr. Bruno Stojic, and that's when I learnt that Mr. Bruno Stojic no longer occupied that post but that it was Perica Jukic. That's what they were -- that's what they told me in the building where Mr. Bruno Stojic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know where the decisions were made removing those three people from those existing posts?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is something that is unknown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to look at P 07004. I asked you a few moments ago if the practice of forced labour continued after the order issued by Mr. Petkovic. And if you could look, please, at Exhibit 7004. Can you just quickly confirm to us, please, is this again a form of document similar to those we've seen before indicating on the 1st of December, 1993, Mr. Jelic approved the sending out of 30 detainees from the Heliodrom for the purposes of work?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I can ask you to go to the next document, 7107. And is this a similar approval or order for labour dated the 10th of December, 1993, again approved by Mr. Jelic, this time sending out two prisoners from the Heliodrom prison?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the order issued by Mr. Petkovic, it's paragraph -- the last paragraph number 3, said something to the effect that anyone violating his order would be held accountable. To your knowledge, sir - of course, we can only ask for what you know - did you ever know anyone to be punished, disciplined, prosecuted, dismissed for the use of forced labour after Mr. Petkovic's order or at any time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't know that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you know of anyone -- were any of are officers, were any of your military police officers disciplined or removed because they had been involved in forced labour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I would like only to ask the witness that to your question Mr. Scott he answered in English on the transcript that, "I could not know that at all." My question is, if you could not know about it because you were in a way prevented to do so or to be able to know about it, or you did not know about it, meaning that if you did not know if anybody was in a way taken to the courts or to any other level of criminal punishment. So my question is, if you did not know or if you could not know -- if you could not know about those measures, disciplinary measures, et cetera, then why you could not or should not know about them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My work post was related just to Heliodrom, nothing else. So there's no way I could have known what was going on elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me follow up on that, sir. But you've shown us today and we've looked at a number of documents where you were raising, if I can say you were waving the flag on this as well as other issues, the use of forced labour, the wounding of prisoners. Weren't you interested or curious to know if anyone in the HVO was being punished or disciplined in connection with that behaviour?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We cannot know in the prison why somebody was condemned and convicted to serve a sentence. All we know is that they came. Now, why they came, why they were there, what they had done and so on, we didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In relation to a document that I'm going to show you in a moment, can you confirm that, in connection with the arrest that started on the 30th of June, 1993, were some Muslim women arrested and held at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were few women who were placed in the prison building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say a few, can you give us your best estimate of a number, please?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't be exact, but four or five women perhaps. I can't remember. I know there was some.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us where in the Heliodrom facility were these women held or confined?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were physically separated from the others, the prisoners of war and the military prisoners, and they were confined on the second floor where -- and the key to that area, only the security commander had the key to that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when you say "security commander" now, are you referring to Mr. Smiljanic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you come to know in the fall of 1993 that these five women apparently had been released?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but before I come to that, did you ever understand any reason or basis for why these women were being held?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, we don't know what the reason for their incarceration was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, perhaps to be very, very safe, Your Honour, we should go into private session for one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you've made several references today to a report or a communication that you sent to Mr. Stojic and to Mr. Naletilic, Tuta. As we will see and I will ask the courtroom to turn to P 06170. Did you include in your -- in that letter your concern about the fact that these people had been released and how that had happened?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I arrived back from sick leave, in talking to Snjezana Cvitanovic and having an insight into the documents, I happened to notice that a group of female detainees, including (redacted) had been released, but on that list all it said was -- all it had was the signature of Mr. Berko Pusic. Now, since release from prison is something that I could consider nobody could permit without having previously been granted permission and with agreement of Zvonko Vidovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise to the witness for interruption, but even though we've done it in any event out of an abundance of caution, could we ask for a redaction, please, of Ms. (redacted) name. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Registrar, issue an order to have that name redacted. Line 16, page 78.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you were telling us about the letter that -- the communication you were discussing with your secretary Ms. Cvitanovic. Could you just continue on, please, but you need not mention probably the names of any particular prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Snjezana -- Snjezana Cvitanovic showed me some documents where I saw this document too. However, the signatory of this document on the release was the signature of Berislav Pusic. Now, since there was no previous document, a previous document was lacking about release from prison, we weren't able to see any agreement. We weren't able to see the agreement given by SIS and the crime prevention service of the military police. That is why I considered that this was irregular release and I wrote the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I just ask you to very briefly look back at -- I believe it would be the immediately preceding document in the bundle, P 05952. And again, perhaps it might be best again if we didn't broadcast the document outside the courtroom, and I'll just ask you, Witness, not to mention any of the names on the document, but can you just simply confirm to us that this is an approval signed by -- well, apparently over the name of Mr. Pusic, dated the 19th of October, 1993, and is this part of what you were complaining about in your letter to Mr. Stojic and Mr. Tuta?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back to your actual letter to Mr. Stojic and Mr. Tuta -- or Mr. Naletilic I suppose I should say, 6170. Once you prepare the letter, which we have in front us, could you tell us -- tell the Judges, please, how did you go back delivering that to Mr. Stojic and Mr. Naletilic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The letter that I wrote I personally took and handed over to the secretary of Mr. Bruno Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall where that office was located at the time when you delivered the letter there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to explain it. It was in town, and perhaps the briefest way to tell you is along the Partisan cemetery -- or by the Partisan cemetery in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say "town" you're referring to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What made you, by the way, decide to not only provide this report to Mr. Stojic but to also provide the same report to Mr. Naletilic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I considered that Mr. Bruno Stojic was the president of the office, and that Mr. Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, was an advisor to Mr. Bruno Stojic for security matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me stop you for a moment, please. When you say that you considered that Mr. Stojic was president of the office, can you tell us a bit more about what you mean by that? Or maybe it's translation, I'm not sure, but what position are you ascribing to Mr. Stojic when you say that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the head, the head of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And you said that Mr. Naletilic was an advisor to Mr. Stojic for security matters?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you know where Mr. Tuta's -- sorry, Mr. Naletilic's office was in that capacity in relationship to Mr. Stojic's office?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you enter the building, on that first floor, on the right-hand side was Mr. Bruno Stojic's office, and straight from the stairs on there was the office of Mr. Mladen Naletilic, Tuta. They were next to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you personally hand your report, which is reflected in Exhibit 6170, to the secretary for Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us -- again, I'll ask, do you recall ever receiving a response from either Mr. Stojic or Mr. Naletilic to your report?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just before we leave this document, unless the Judges have additional questions, your report or letter itself, you refer at the very beginning to the order of the 10th of August establishing the commission and appointing you to it. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you then to go to Exhibit 6848. And can you tell us what this document is, please?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was drafted right afterwards, shortly afterwards, at the same time were I addressed all the things that were happening at Heliodrom and asking for assistance to improve the conditions there and to improve our work. Some important things were emphasised, namely, that the shortage of security personnel needs to be addressed, that security needs to be enforced to make the prison safer. In this document I also draw their attention to the fact that Major General Milivoj Petkovic prohibited the handing over of prisoners for labour, and Mr. Stanko Bozic obeyed this order and demanded that all the detainees, who had left to do some labour and had not been returned, be brought back. At the time of this letter, the time of this report, there were still some detainees who had not been brought back, and this was also filed in the archives of the prison. I also stress that Mr. Stanko Bozic, in concurrence with the then brigade commander, allowed those people to go out to work in logistical bases, workshops, the kitchen, to clean the town, to clean streets, the barracks, et cetera. However, from individual sources, I cannot know which, news had reached me that those prisoners were allegedly taken outside the perimeter of Heliodrom, and outside Heliodrom there were cases of escape, injuries, and deaths. I learned that from people who simply told me about it. I also mention here that one prisoner escaped from a place called Vrde, from a group that was taken away by the brigade led by Stanko or Ranko Boban. I demanded that steps be taken immediately to improve the work of the prison and to improve -- to improve security and safety and to finally clear up who was authorised to approve releases of prisoners to work who had authority over the central prison of Mostar. And I addressed that to Mr. Roso, Mr. Lavric, and Perica Jukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On that last point, sir, we see that in the original Croatian language version, we can see that the name Bruno Stojic has been stricken through and above it has been handwritten "Perica Jukic." Is that a change that you made to the document or, to your knowledge, is that something that somebody else did after it left your hands?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Snjezana typed this report, and when we were about to send it off somebody said that Mr. Bruno Stojic was no longer in that position, and then I wrote in my own hand the name that I was told, although I had never seen that gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you before turning to a couple of final topics whether during 1993 -- let me back up, please. You testified yesterday, I believe, that Mr. Coric came to the Heliodrom prison when Mr. Stanko Bozic was installed as warden in about December 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: After that time, and it's between that time and the end of -- or late 1993 or at the date of your report to Mr. Roso and others dated the 24th of November, 1993, to your knowledge, had you ever seen Mr. Coric at the Heliodrom prison ever again between December 1992 and the end of November 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. Never. He never came.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can I ask a similar question about Mr. Stojic. Just during 1993, can you tell the Judges any occasion that you recall meeting or seeing Mr. Stojic at the Heliodrom prison?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Bruno Stojic never came to Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you understand when you were appointed to this commission in August that the commission extended not only as to Heliodrom but also related to other HVO prisons such as, for example, Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Ibrisimovic, microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness already answered, but I do object to this line of questioning. The question is -- the witness is being led.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir -- can you tell the Judges about any transfers of prisoners between Ljubuski and Heliodrom that you may recall?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall a number of people with regard to which Stanko Bozic entrusted me with admitting those people who were supposed to arrive from Ljubuski. It was rather a large group, perhaps 200 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you know any particular prisoner who was ever transferred -- an individual prisoner who was transferred from the Heliodrom to Ljubuski during 1993? I mean a personal acquaintance. Not just someone you knew the name, but someone that you knew personally.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hamdija Jahic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How did you know Mr. Jahic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He used to work before the war at the municipality in Mostar, and we had known each other for many years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges, has he held any position in Mostar either currently or in the last few years in a senior government position?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the head of a legal department in the municipal government. That's all I knew. But I think it had something to do with town planning in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Forgive me, my question probably wasn't very clear. More recently, either today or in the last year or so, has Mr. Jahic been the mayor of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I take it -- is it correct that Mr. Jahic is a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges anything more you can recall about the time that he was transferred from the Heliodrom to Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that he didn't go on his own. There was an order that I hadn't seen to move a group of detainees to the Ljubuski prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you hear these -- this particular group described in any particular way or anything that marked or identified this particular group of people that were transferred along with Mr. Jahic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not described in any particular way, but I saw them. I didn't know their names. I just recognised him. I think that this group was a group of more educated people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And going to the HVO -- excuse me, facility at Dretelj, were you still working at the Heliodrom in late 1993 when any prisoners were brought there from Dretelj and, if so, can you tell us what you saw at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since it was a very hot season -- it was very, very hot when those prisoners were moved to Heliodrom by trucks. They got off near the school building. There they were admitted and listed and put up in the school building or inside gyms and halls.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was the appearance or condition of these prisoners when you saw them come off the trucks at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of that heat and how they got there travelling in covered trucks, of course they were sweaty, unshaven, dishevelled, and unkempt. When I came close I felt an unpleasant smell.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I asked you yesterday that -- how you felt on the 9th of May, 1993, when you saw these women and children coming into the Heliodrom. Let me ask you a similar question now. When you saw these men arrive from Dretelj, how did you feel about that? How did it make you feel?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It made me feel bad because I ran into a neighbour of mine, a man who lived in the same apartment building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: He was one of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was his condition like, and did he say anything to you at the time or afterwards?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since I knew the man, his name was Zijo Maksumic, and we were close, and we were good neighbours, always courteous to each other. I asked him, "How are you faring Zijo?" And he was silent for a while before he said, and I quote, "Just spend one day in Dretelj and you'll find out." That was our entire conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, did you find that -- or can you tell us that in approximately December 1993 a number of the HVO prisons or detention facilities were closed?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us anything about the decisions or actions that led up to the camps being closed, or is that something you cannot help us with?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about other prisons, only Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you learn at some time, then, that as to the Heliodrom prison, a number of prisoners, a large number of prisoners would be released?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just tell us what happened at that time. Again, did this have anything to do with the classification or categories of prisoners, and what happened in connection with these people actually leaving the facility?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Larger groups that left the prison were subject to a procedure involving officials of the office for exchanges and the International Red Cross. The ICRC was present at all those large releases. Everybody was released in that period except for those prisoners against whom criminal reports were filed, and they remained and were moved to the prison building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you give to the Judges any information, please, as to when you say everybody was released in that period except for those prisoners against whom criminal reports were filed, approximately, of the total number of men or people who were still held at the Heliodrom as of December 1993, what percentage or what number were actually kept or actually kept behind, if you will, as persons against whom criminal reports were pending?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the number, and I don't want to venture a figure, but I can say that all of them could fit into the prison building, the one that was meant to be a prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So the number was sufficiently small that you didn't have to use the school or the sports hall any more to hold these prisoners against whom military -- excuse me, criminal reports were pending; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, it's time. There is a hearing in this courtroom after us. I think you have about 30 minutes to conclude tomorrow. That would allow the Defence to use up all their time, and they have to be careful about that. Tomorrow, Mr. Scott, therefore, you have 30 minutes to conclude. Witness, you will return tomorrow at 9.00 a.m., and until that time, as I said yesterday, you are not going to meet with or talk with anybody. Is there anything to add, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, except to say that I hope to actually not need the 30 minutes, but I do think there will be a few remaining items. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I thank you in advance for that. So until tomorrow at 9.00 a.m. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
